summary: Defines how to carry Timed Text Markup Language (TTML), the W3C XML-based timed text format used for subtitles and captions, in Real-time Transport Protocol packets. It targets streaming workflows.

eli5.summary: Subtitles for a video are sent as little notes timed with the picture. This explains how to package them into live streaming packets.

subtitle: How to carry TTML subtitles and closed captions inside RTP packets for streaming workflows.

tldr.problem: Television and streaming workflows need to send subtitles and closed captions as live text, but earlier RTP text formats were too limited or aimed at other uses.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries a 16-bit Length and then User Data Words holding all or part of one TTML document. The RTP Timestamp is the moment the document becomes active, and the marker bit flags the last packet of a document.
tldr.outcome: TTML can be streamed over RTP with simple timing, fragmentation and loss-protection rules. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8759 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TTML Needs an RTP Payload Format
sections.content:
TTML (Timed Text Markup Language) is a W3C media type that describes timed text, such as closed captions and subtitles, as XML. RFC 8759 says how to map TTML into an RTP stream for streaming workflows, including those in the European Broadcasting Union's EBU-TT Part 3 specification. It does not define a new media type and reuses application/ttml+xml.

The RFC explains why older text formats do not fit. RFC 4103 is for low data rate conversation with its own session management and minimal formatting. RFC 4734 deals largely with fax and modem signalling. RFC 4396 carries a timed text format with far more restricted formatting than TTML. With no existing format for TTML or generic XML, a new payload format was needed.
sections.eli5: Older ways to send text over a live stream were built for chats or fax machines, not TV subtitles. So this RFC makes a new envelope just for subtitles.

sections.title: The Packet Layout
sections.content:
After the usual RTP header, the payload holds a 16-bit Reserved field, a 16-bit Length field and the User Data Words, which are the TTML text. Each RTP payload contains one TTML document or part of one.

The RTP header fields follow RFC 3550 with a few specifics. The marker bit is set to 1 on the last packet of a document, and otherwise 0; the first packet may also be the last. The timestamp encodes the epoch of the document. A document spread over several packets MUST use the same timestamp with different consecutive sequence numbers, and sequential documents MUST NOT share a timestamp. Because packets do not represent a constant duration, the timestamp cannot be used to infer packet loss.

Reserved MUST be set to 0x0 and ignored on reception. Length is the size of the User Data Words in bytes and MUST match what is actually carried. Characters that take more than one byte MUST be serialised in big-endian (network byte order).
sections.eli5: Each packet is an envelope with a label saying how long the note inside is. A flag marks the envelope holding the end of a note, and all envelopes for one note share the same time stamp.

sections.title: Content Restrictions on Carried Documents
sections.content:
Multiple TTML subtitle streams MUST NOT be interleaved in a single RTP stream. The document's root tt element MUST include a timeBase attribute in the http://www.w3.org/ns/ttml#parameter namespace with the value media.

The RFC also expresses this as a minimal TTML2 content profile, designated urn:ietf:rfc:8759#content. It marks #timeBase-media as required and #timeBase-smpte and #timeBase-clock as prohibited. Documents carried over RTP MUST conform to it in addition to any other profiles they use.

Other TTML profiles may limit how complex the changes are, and deployments may limit how long a document can last. The RFC treats both as out of scope.
sections.eli5: Every subtitle note must say that its timing is measured by the video's own clock, not by a wall clock. That keeps everything in step with the picture.

sections.title: How Receivers Process Documents
sections.content:
An invalid document MUST be discarded, and this includes empty documents of zero length. Each valid document becomes active at its epoch E, which MUST be the RTP Timestamp of the packet carrying it. Media times inside the document are offset relative to E.

At any moment on the RTP time line, exactly zero or one document SHALL be active. If document D(n-1) is active and D(n) arrives with a later epoch, processing of D(n-1) MUST stop at E(n) and D(n) MUST begin. A document MAY be stopped earlier once all of its defined content has ended.

Because the timestamp does not give exact media timing and documents can be fragmented, the RTCP jitter calculation is unusable for this payload format.

The RFC also defines a feature extension, urn:ietf:rfc:8759#rtp-relative-media-time, and a minimal TTML2 processor profile. Receivers MUST support the features marked required there, which does not mean they must support full TTML1 or TTML2 profile processing. The codecs media type parameter MUST name at least one processor profile compatible with this one.
sections.eli5: Only one subtitle note is on screen at a time. When a newer note arrives, it takes over from the older one at its start time.

sections.title: Fragmentation of Large Documents
sections.content:
Many TTML uses are low bit rate and fit in one packet within the Path MTU, but some documents are larger and may be split across packets. When fragmenting, documents SHOULD be split into as few fragments as possible (the RFC says this is RECOMMENDED). Text strings MUST be split at character boundaries so partial documents can be decoded, which means the sender must understand the UTF-8 or UTF-16 encoding to find boundaries.

The receiver rebuilds the document by concatenating the User Data Words of consecutive packets in ascending sequence number order. Only one document may be sent for a given RTP Timestamp. The packet after one with the marker bit set begins a new document.
sections.eli5: If a note is too long for one envelope, it is split into several. The split must happen between letters, never in the middle of one, and the receiver glues the pieces back in order.

sections.title: Loss Protection and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Acceptable document loss depends on the TTML profile and use case, so the RFC sets no specific limits. Documents MAY be sent without extra protection if end-to-end network conditions guarantee loss stays acceptable under all anticipated load. Otherwise implementations MUST use a protection mechanism, such as forward error correction (RFC 5109), retransmission (RFC 4588), duplication, or an equivalent technique.

Congestion control follows RFC 3550 and any applicable RTP profile. Applications MUST comply with RFC 8083, with particular attention to its Section 4.4 on Media Usability. RFC 8085 gives further guidance for UDP streams.
sections.eli5: Lost subtitle packets mean missing words. So unless the network is very reliable, senders must send extra copies or repair data, and they must also slow down when the network gets crowded.

sections.title: Clock Rate and SDP Mapping
sections.content:
The payload format uses the existing application/ttml+xml media type. The default clock rate is 1000 Hz. It SHOULD be included in any advertisement of the stream. When choosing a rate, implementers should consider related video or audio, and it is RECOMMENDED to share the same clock source and rate as that media.

For the Session Description Protocol, the mapping follows Section 3 of RFC 4855. The type name application goes in the m= line, the subtype ttml+xml and the clock rate go in a=rtpmap, and the other parameters go in a=fmtp as a semicolon-separated list. The codecs parameter MUST be included there.
sections.eli5: The stream's clock ticks 1000 times a second unless it says otherwise. A short description sent before the stream starts tells receivers what kind of data to expect and how fast the clock runs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These packets inherit the security considerations of RTP and its profiles, and applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong security mechanisms. Choosing them is the job of whoever uses RTP, not of the payload format.

Receivers should check that the User Data Words match the Length field to avoid buffer overflow attacks. The format places no restriction on document size, so malicious senders could attempt denial of service; senders should avoid producing DoS-like streams and receivers should avoid mistaking legitimate streams for attacks. As with other XML types, repeated expansion of maliciously constructed XML entities can use up memory. TTML itself has no active or executable content, and the RFC says XML signatures or encryption are not normally expected.
sections.eli5: Receivers should check that a note is really as long as its label says, and not accept absurdly huge notes, so nobody can overload them.

data.title: RTP header and TTML payload header

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Set to 1 on the last packet of a document.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Consecutive numbers for packets of one document.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: Epoch of the TTML document; the same for all its packets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be 0x0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of User Data Words in bytes.

data.title: SDP for TTML over RTP
data.code:
m=application 30000 RTP/AVP 112
a=rtpmap:112 ttml+xml/90000
a=fmtp:112 charset=utf-8;codecs=im2t
